1 │ # The printed form of my classes puts angle brackets around the name
   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ 
   5 │ When I look at an object in the console or in a debugger, the text the library builds for me has angle brackets wrapped around the class name and its values. A class holding x and y shows up as <C(x=1, y=2)>, and a class with no values at all shows up as <C3()>. Those brackets add noise right next to the name, and the examples on the front page and in the guide on why you would use the library all show that same bracketed form.
   6 │ 
   7 │ ## What should happen
   8 │ 
   9 │ The text for an object should show the class name and its values plainly, with no angle brackets. The same object should appear as C(x=1, y=2), and the class with no values should appear as C3(). The front page and the guide should show the plain form too, so the words match what I actually see.
  10 │ 
  11 │ ## About this project
  12 │ 
  13 │ attrs is a Python package whose decorators write the repetitive parts of a class for you. You list the values your data class holds, and the library writes the starter, the comparison, the hash, and a readable printed form for that class.
  14 │ 
  15 │ ## Problem this solves
  16 │ 
  17 │ The brackets make every printed object clutter, and the project's own guide says they add ambiguity when you are trying to read a value while debugging. I want to look at an object and read a plain name and a list of values, with nothing extra around the name.
  18 │ 
  19 │ ## What changed
  20 │ 
  21 │ Objects made with this library now print their class name and values without the surrounding angle brackets. The front page example and the guide on why you would use the library were updated to show the plain form, including the hand-written comparison example in the guide. The bracketed form is no longer produced by the library at all.
  22 │ 
  23 │ ## Impact
  24 │ 
  25 │ This is a visible change in usability: the printed form of every class the library builds loses the brackets. Anything you compare against that text, such as saved output, examples in your own notes, or a check in your own test suite, has to expect the plain form. The values, the comparisons, the hash, and the starter are untouched.

   3 │ Why not…
   4 │ ========
   5 │ 
   6 │ 
   7 │ …tuples?
   8 │ --------
   9 │ 
  10 │ 
  11 │ Readability
  12 │ ^^^^^^^^^^^
  13 │

  23 │

  27 │ 
  28 │ or::

  30 │    (42, 23, "Jane", "John")
  31 │ 
  32 │ ?
  33 │ 
  34 │ Why would you want to write ``customer[2]`` instead of ``customer.first_name``?
  35 │ 
  36 │ Don't get me started when you add nesting.
  37 │ If you've never ran into mysterious tuples you had no idea what the hell they meant while debugging, you're much smarter then I am.
  38 │ 
  39 │ Using proper classes with names and types makes program code much more readable and comprehensible_.
  40 │ Especially when trying to grok a new piece of software or returning to old code after several months.
  41 │ 
  42 │ .. _comprehensible: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.5257.pdf
  43 │ 
  44 │ 
  45 │ Extendability
  46 │ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  47 │ 
  48 │ Imagine you have a function that takes or returns a tuple.
  49 │ Especially if you use tuple unpacking (eg. ``x, y = get_point()``), adding additional data means that you have to change the invocation of that function *everywhere*.
  50 │ 
  51 │ Adding an attribute to a class concerns only those who actually care about that attribute.
  52 │ 
  53 │ 
  54 │ …namedtuples?
  55 │ -------------
  56 │ 
  57 │ The difference between :func:`collections.namedtuple`\ s and classes decorated by ``attrs`` is that the latter are type-sensitive and less typing aside regular classes:
  58 │ 
  59 │ 
  60 │ .. doctest::
  61 │ 
  62 │    >>> import attr
  63 │    >>> @attr.s
  64 │    ... class C1(object):
  65 │    ...     a = attr.ib()
  66 │    ...     def print_a(self):
  67 │    ...        print self.a
  68 │    >>> @attr.s
  69 │    ... class C2(object):
  70 │    ...     a = attr.ib()
  71 │    >>> c1 = C1(a=1)
  72 │    >>> c2 = C2(a=1)
  73 │    >>> c1.a == c2.a
  74 │    True
  75 │    >>> c1 == c2
  76 │    False
  77 │    >>> c1.print_a()
  78 │    1
  79 │ 
  80 │ 
  81 │ …while namedtuple’s purpose is *explicitly* to behave like tuples:
  82 │ 
  83 │ 
  84 │ .. doctest::
  85 │ 
  86 │    >>> from collections import namedtuple
  87 │    >>> NT1 = namedtuple("NT1", "a")
  88 │    >>> NT2 = namedtuple("NT2", "b")
  89 │    >>> t1 = NT1._make([1,])
  90 │    >>> t2 = NT2._make([1,])
  91 │    >>> t1 == t2 == (1,)
  92 │    True
  93 │ 
  94 │ 
  95 │ This can easily lead to surprising and unintended behaviors.
  96 │ 
  97 │ Other than that, ``attrs`` also adds nifty features like validators or default values.
  98 │ 
  99 │ .. _tuple: https://docs.python.org/2/tutorial/datastructures.html#tuples-and-sequences
 100 │

"""Extract and run the doctest blocks from a .rst file, block by block."""
import doctest

import sys
import textwrap

path = sys.argv[1]
lines = open(path).read().splitlines()

            cur.append(line)
        else:

runner = doctest.DocTestRunner(optionflags=doctest.ELLIPSIS)
parser = doctest.DocTestParser()
total_fail = 0
for i, block in enumerate(blocks, 1):
    src = textwrap.dedent("\n".join(block))
    if not src.strip():
        continue
    if not re.search(r">>>", src):
        print("block %d: skipped (no >>> example)" % i)
        continue
    test = parser.get_doctest(src, {}, path, path, i)
    out = []
    res = runner.run(test, out=out.append)
    total_fail += res.failed
    status = "OK" if res.failed == 0 else "FAILED"
    print("block %d: %s (%d examples)" % (i, status, res.attempted))
    for chunk in out:
        sys.stdout.write(chunk)

"""Extract and run the doctest blocks from .rst files, block by block."""
import doctest
import re
import sys
import textwrap

sys.path.insert(0, "/workspace")

runner = doctest.DocTestRunner(optionflags=doctest.ELLIPSIS)
for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    lines = open(path).read().splitlines()

    blocks = []
    cur = None
    for line in lines:
        if re.match(r"\s*\.\. doctest::\s*$", line):
            cur = []
            blocks.append(cur)
            continue
        if cur is not None:
            if line.strip() == "" or line.startswith((" ", "\t")):
                cur.append(line)
            else:
                cur = None

    print("=== %s ===" % path)
    total_fail = 0
    for i, block in enumerate(blocks, 1):
        src = textwrap.dedent("\n".join(block))
        if not src.strip() or not re.search(r">>>", src):
            continue
        test = parser.get_doctest(">>> import attr\n" + src, {}, path, path, i)
        out = []
        res = runner.run(test, out=out.append)
        total_fail += res.failed
        status = "OK" if res.failed == 0 else "FAILED"
        print("block %d: %s (%d examples)" % (i, status, res.attempted))
        for chunk in out:
            sys.stdout.write(chunk)
